Ben Gvir’s Human Resources Department From Hell

Itamar Ben Gvir just turned prison oversight into a loyalty test written in blood.

Under the new setup, the National Security Minister has formally cut the number of “official inspectors” for security prisoners to fewer than 20 and handed six of those slots to members of bereaved families from the Choosing Life forum, whose children were killed in Palestinian attacks. These are not ceremonial escorts. 

Under the Death Penalty for Terrorists Law, inspectors get real supervisory authority over conditions and implementation, including the right to be present at executions once the bill is fully in force.

This is the logical next step in a three‑year policy of turning prisons into a political stage. Ben Gvir has already paraded through Ofer Prison with victims’ relatives and the prison service chief while cameras rolled, as heavily armed guards stormed corridors, fired stun grenades and forced bound Palestinian detainees face‑down on the floor. 

He then pushed the footage himself, boasting that “terrorists” are finally in “real prisons, not hotels,” and openly saying, surrounded by piled‑up prisoners, that what he really wants is to execute them.

What disappears in this script is any notion of neutral oversight. Family visits are cut back, Red Cross access is attacked, human rights groups are smeared, and when courts or professionals raise questions about torture, medical neglect or due process, the answer is to wheel in grieving parents with official badges and call that justice. 

In sovereignty terms, the state is blurring one of its most dangerous powers — to cage and kill — into raw, personalized vengeance, wrapping it in grief that cannot be argued with.

It’s a politics that does two things at once. Outwardly, it sells the death penalty as “choosing life,” with golden noose pins in the Knesset and campaign videos in front of gallows. Inwardly, it hollows out the line between law and revenge. 

The message to the prison system is simple: you are no longer enforcing a state standard; you are acting out a narrative for an audience that has already decided the only acceptable ending.

Congress has not yet seen the text of the Iran memorandum of understanding, even as Trump says he intends to submit it for legislative approval, according to the Times of Israel. American law may require congressional sign-off, but several Republican members say they have received nothing - creating an unusual situation where the administration is promising a vote on a document its own party hasn't read.

Some GOP lawmakers are already signaling frustration. The dynamic matters: even a handful of Republican defections could complicate ratification, giving hardliners leverage they haven't formally exercised yet.

Whether Trump sends the full MOU or a summary will likely determine how much of a fight he faces from within his own caucus.
